title: How to keep reading
hookLine: a few lines a day, one line carried: the way to read any old book

cards: There's a kind of book that ends up on a nightstand. Big, old, bought in a burst of good intention, read for three nights, then used as a coaster. Maybe the problem isn't the book, or the reader.
Maybe it's the method. Old books get read the way the news gets read: fast, for information, all at once. They were never written for that.
For seventy-odd days this camp has read two old books a few lines at a time. Today, lectio divina.

teach.b: The Roman writer Seneca, a Stoic who wrote long before Marcus, gives this advice in his second letter to his friend Lucilius. Don't wander through piles of authors. Stay with a few great ones and digest them.
Food that comes straight back up nourishes no one. In Richard Gummere's 1917 translation, he puts it in three words: "Everywhere means nowhere." Then Seneca describes his own habit.
Each day, out of everything he reads, he picks one thought to chew on for the rest of the day.

And in that very letter he does it, picking a line from another philosopher, Epicurus, about poverty that's content being an honorable thing. One thought, carried. Christian monks worked out something similar.
A medieval Carthusian monk named Guigo described a ladder of four steps for reading scripture slowly: reading, then turning the words over, then prayer, then resting in silence.

It's called lectio divina, holy reading, and it is still practiced today. Different aims, different sources, the same rhythm: slow, little, and kept. So here's a method for any old book, sacred or not.

teach.h: READ SLOWLY, PICK ONE, CARRY IT.
teach.b: Read them slowly, twice. Pick one phrase. Carry it until evening.
Three lines a day is more than a thousand lines a year. The Meditations, the Masnavi, the Psalms, the Gita, the Dhammapada: none of them has to be finished on a weekend.

how: Some readers of old texts read a few lines a day and carry one phrase, as Seneca describes in his second letter; Christians who keep lectio divina read scripture in the same slow way.

games.q: you want to read the Meditations properly. what do you do?
o: three lines a day, one phrase carried.
games.why: Seneca picked one thought a day and chewed on it; the monks read slowly in four steps. little, slow and kept is the habit both describe.

practice: If there's a book nearby, open it anywhere and take three lines; if not, use three lines you know by heart. Read or say them one at a time, word by word, as if each word cost money.
Then go back, let one phrase rise, and hold just that phrase for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: Lectio divina. The monks' slow way of reading scripture: read, turn the words over, pray, then rest in silence. Today's word.
